cim: Artificial intelligence adoption and occupational well-being in higher education management: evidence from universities in Guangzhou
cim_eredeti: Artificial intelligence adoption and occupational well-being in higher education management: evidence from universities in Guangzhou
szoveg_eredeti:
Volume 17 - 2026 | https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1931597

1. International Education School, Guangzhou College of Technology and Business, Guangzhou, China

2. Faculty of Entrepreneurship and Business, Universiti Malaysia Kelantan, Kota Bharu, Kelantan, Malaysia

Universities are increasingly introducing artificial intelligence (AI) tools into administrative and managerial work. Yet evidence on how AI adoption relates to occupational well-being in higher education management remains fragmented. Building on the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model and contemporary technostress scholarship, this study examines direct, indirect, and conditional associations between AI adoption and occupational well-being in university management in Guangzhou.

The cross-sectional questionnaire dataset contained 320 complete records and was analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM), with a two-stage interaction specification and 5,000 bootstrap resamples.

AI adoption was positively associated with technostress, which was negatively associated with occupational well-being. Neither the direct AI adoption-well-being association nor the conditional total association at mean organizational support was statistically significant. The negative indirect association through technostress was significant at that support level. Perceived organizational support was positively associated with well-being and with a weaker negative technostress-well-being association. The model explained 23.04% of technostress variance and 10.69% of well-being variance.

These results support a statistical stress pathway but do not establish a direct well-being benefit of AI adoption. Cross-sectional associations do not establish causal mechanisms. The study contributes an occupational well-being perspective to AI-enabled university administration and identifies training, workload redesign, and organizational support as priorities for future evaluation.

Across higher education systems, administrative functions are being transformed through data-rich decision making, automation of routine tasks and introduction of AI-powered tools like chatbots, document drafting tools, predictive analytics (enrollment and retention), and algorithmic workflow triage (Crompton and Burke, 2023). These tools promise faster service delivery and improved managerial control, yet they may also alter job demands, skill requirements and accountability structures in a way that can have an impact on staff well-being (Zawacki-Richter et al., 2019; Zirar et al., 2023; Valtonen et al., 2025).

Occupational well-being has been defined as sustained positive functioning in the work environment, often manifested as affective states (e.g., vitality, calmness), evaluative judgments (e.g., satisfaction) and low levels of strain and risk of burnout. Recent studies of AI in the workplace are increasingly referring to AI as a ‘double-edged sword’ in terms of well-being, with the benefits of AI depending on self-efficacy, task fit and organizational support (Kim and Lee, 2024; Aulia and Lin, 2025; Valtonen et al., 2025).

Guangzhou provides the geographical context for the manuscript’s focus on university administrative and managerial work. University management work is a relevant setting for studying these dynamics because it involves high information loads, frequent interaction with stakeholders and stringent compliance requirements. In such settings, it is possible to consider the uptake of AI as a new resource (e.g., cognitive support, error reduction, and speed) and a new demand (e.g., learning burden, monitoring pressure, and ambiguity about responsibility for AI-assisted decisions; Chuang et al., 2025; Mansuroğlu and Smith, 2026; Bankins et al., 2024). However, much of the AI-in-higher-education literature addresses teaching and learning, leaving the occupational experiences of administrative professionals less extensively examined (Bond et al., 2024).

This study therefore asks three questions: (RQ1) Is AI adoption directly associated with occupational well-being among higher education managers? (RQ2) Is AI adoption indirectly associated with occupational well-being through technostress? (RQ3) Does the technostress–well-being association differ according to perceived organizational support? Addressing these questions may inform responsible AI adoption in university administration, without assuming that cross-sectional associations identify the effects of specific implementation practices (Bankins et al., 2024; Zirar et al., 2023).

AI Adoption in Higher Education Management describes the degree to which the managers and professional staff regularly employ artificial intelligence-enabled tools to carry out their regular core duties like planning, reporting, policy drafting, resource allocation and communicating with stakeholders. This adoption involves not only technical use but also trust, perceived utility, and the incorporation of AI’s outputs into decision routines (Zirar et al., 2023; Bankins et al., 2024; Aulia and Lin, 2025).

Recent research suggests that the adoption of AI can lead to increased performance and better subjective well-being if the tasks are tailored to the technology, support human expertise and algorithmic recommendations (Cramarenco et al., 2023). However, adoption can also increase workload in terms of faster cycles of communication, greater expectations of responsiveness, and greater levels of monitoring, particularly when AI is introduced without redesigning workflows.

Within socio-technical views, AI adoption can be viewed as a system-level change. The same AI tool can potentially be used as a resource for one role (e.g., policy analysts) and a demand for another (e.g., frontline student services) - depending on autonomy, training and governance. This framing is in line with multi-level reviews highlighting that the human experience of workplace AI depends on the choices made during the implementation process and not just on the technology itself (Bankins et al., 2024; Mansuroğlu and Smith, 2026; Zirar et al., 2023).

Technostress describes the stress that people feel when they have trouble coping with the demands posed by technology (Tarafdar et al., 2019). Contemporary reviews emphasize that technostress is multidimensional, including overload, invasion in nonwork time, complexity, insecurity, and uncertainty (Borle et al., 2021).

AI may introduce distinctive technostressors through opaque decision logic, frequent version changes, and perceived threats of substitution. Even when AI is intended to augment employees’ work, uncertainty about outputs and evaluations may contribute to role ambiguity. These possibilities are consistent with research on AI-related insecurity and self-efficacy, but should be distinguished from mechanisms measured directly in a particular study (Kim and Lee, 2024; Kim and Kim, 2024; Zirar et al., 2023; Högemann et al., 2025).

Research based on the concept of technostress for education and public services has found consistent associations between high digital demands and low flourishing, engagement, and well-being, while organizational resources, including supportive leadership, training, and clear policies, are relevant to employees’ responses (Harunavamwe and Ward, 2022; Pansini et al., 2023).

Occupational well-being is frequently described in terms of the JD-R model in which job demands are believed to tax energy and cause strain, while job resources facilitate motivation, engagement and health. This framework has been extensively used in education, including higher education (Bakker and Demerouti, 2017; Mudrak et al., 2018; Naidoo-Chetty and Du Plessis, 2021).
